messages.author: d79deff2ac4a4c6a
messages.subject: Python Question?
parts:
Hey everyone -

I know that this is technically an R group, but I have a quick and specific question in Python if anyone has any Python experience…I just need to convert a file from a certain format that I generate in a data simulation to a netCDF file, and I have the GitHub page with the code. I’m also attaching some sample files to convert, although I do have the real one (it’s just much bigger).

https://github.com/GrumpyNounours/Nefis2netcdf

 I’ve just never used Python. Any help would be appreciated - cookies may or may not be offered in compensation! 

Thanks!

Alex

messages.author: d567d0ef3c054a35
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Python Question?
parts:
Hi, Alex. I took a quick look at this but was unable to find a
solution, but i think the problem is more in assembling a consistent
set of Python packages than in writing the Python code. Something
like the attached document would probably work, *if* you had the right
set of packages. (Note that I have no idea what the relationship is,
if any, between the ".dat" and ".def" files.)

When I do Python these days, I try to use Python 3, but the github
package you cite works only for Python 2. That was the first problem
I encountered. (For instance, Python 2 treated "print" as a kind of
operator, requiring no parentheses, as "print foo", while Python 3
correctly treats "print" as a function, as "print (foo)".)

I tried to patch the github module to read "print (foo)" every place,
but after that I had other problems. For instance, I do have a
"netcdf" module, and I tried modifying the github code to refer to
that (as "from scipy.io import netcdf"), but the author's "netCDF4"
module evidently provides different functionality, compared to my
"netcdf" module. I'm sure there are remaining issues, but I don't
have time to pursue this at the moment.

You might wish to step back from the problem to see if there are other
options: different file formats or different tools. There *are*
netcdf tools available in R, although I don't see any option to write
Nefis-formatted data.

-- Mike

messages.author: 9450fe235592105e
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Python Question?
parts:
Alex, as Mike says, "Python" (Python 2.7) and Python 3 (3.6) are two
different beasts entirely.

With the corollary that I've never coded in python on a Macintosh, but
have done so mostly in Windows (+ a smattering of times in linux), I can
probably help you out. Drop by my office some time (say, after lab
meeting on Monday). You'll "need" to install python 2.7, rather than
P3.6, as trying to get it a 2.7 package to work in P3.6 (as Mike tried)
is typically futile. It's typically simpler if you work on a "clean"
system that doesn't have both 3.6 and 2.7 installed, it would definitely
be possible to have both. But if you, as a non-coder, don't need Python
3 for anything else, just uninstall P3 and keep the innumerable computer
gremlins at bay.

P.S. If anyone else has simple python, perl, PHP, pascal or other
programming questions (particularly a programming parlance prefixed by
"P" 'pparently), feel free to contact me.

--Matt
